newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa arrival rate estimated in wide range.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa arrival rate estimated in wide range.

text.p: Estimates of Ivorian 1996/97 cocoa arrivals vary widely at levels above 100,000 tonnes, and a clear picture may not emerge for two weeks, trade sources said.
Exporters and shipping sources put stocks at Abidjan alone at well over 100,000 tonnes, including carry over from 1995/96.
One source put declared arrivals at 105,000 tonnes, including 63,000 since October 24, when the season was opened.
The source put arrivals in the week to November 8 at 18,000 tonnes, but others said arrivals at San Pedro alone were at least twice that.
"The picture is still not clear and everyone's figures are different. We were waiting for a mid-November take-off," one exporter told Reuters.

Exporters' licences were agreed on Friday. Marketing rates set by the Caistab marketing board on Monday were not expected to be notified to exporters immediately. "There are some final discussions going on today," an exporter said.
This time last year cocoa port stocks were estimated as 110,000 tonnes, with arrivals seen rising to 300,000 by December before a record 1.2 million tonnes by the year's end.
But a shipping rate dispute in 1995 slowed arrivals until mid-November, making comparisons with this year difficult.

Quantities held in up-country stores while bankers held back funds ahead of a government decision on the 1996/97 export licence allocation were unknown, but one source cited a figure of close to 90,000 tonnes.
A crop analyst recently up-country said stocks were high as buyers were busy. Another said, "Arrivals will be heavy when the rates are known. The centre-west is particularly strong."
Exporters and analysts agreed that recent rains along the southern coast would aid late main crop pod development.
Mid-crop pod setting would also be better after a prolonged dry spell had threatened to reduce flower survival, they said.

"Mid-crop flowering is good, not excellent, but still higher than last year," said an analyst. "There could be some small wilting where rains were light but any losses will probably be offset by low incidences of black-pod after the dry conditions."

Black pod, a fungal disease brought on by prolonged damp and cool weather, can ravage crops during the mid-September to December rainy season. But analysts noted there had been very little precipitation during this year's short rainy season.
Pod-counters predict strong November and peak December arrivals before a January tail-off, but exporters and up-country buyers expect a more even spread extending well into early 1997.

Buyers around Gagnoa and exporters in San Pedro said quality was high with moisture problems gone after record July and August rains. "Bean sizes are around 95 (per 100 grams) and the quality is very good. The weather has helped pod sizes and bean drying," said one sopurce.
Arrivals are expected to pick up sharply in the next two weeks, depending on publication of exporter rates."There are large amounts coming through," said one crop analyst.
Estimates for November pivot around 180,000 tonnes, out of an expected total crop of 900,000-950,000.-Abidjan +225 21 90 90
